questions.q: What problem do window functions solve that groupBy() can't?
options: Comparing each row against others in its group while keeping every individual row, rather than collapsing rows into one per group
Window functions can only be used on numeric columns
They remove the need for any aggregation whatsoever
They replace joins entirely
questions.explain: groupBy() collapses many rows into one per group — window functions keep every row while still ranking/comparing.

questions.q: What roles do partitionBy() and orderBy() play inside Window.partitionBy().orderBy()?
options: partitionBy() defines the groups (like groupBy()'s columns), and orderBy() decides the order within each group
They do the exact same thing and either can be omitted freely
orderBy() defines the groups, and partitionBy() decides the order within them
partitionBy() sorts the entire DataFrame regardless of grouping
questions.explain: Together they describe a per-row "neighborhood" without collapsing anything.

options: Numbers each row 1, 2, 3... within its own partition, in the order the window's orderBy() specified
Counts the total number of rows in the entire DataFrame
Returns the row's position in the original, unsorted file
Removes every row except the very first one in the DataFrame
questions.explain: The .over(window) part is what tells Spark to apply the ranking per-window instead of across the whole DataFrame.

questions.q: How do window functions properly solve the problem Lesson 52 flagged with dropDuplicates()?
options: By ranking duplicates with row_number() using a specific order, then keeping only the rows where the rank equals 1
Window functions cannot address that problem at all
By calling dropDuplicates() a second time
By deleting the entire partition whenever a tie is found
questions.explain: This gives control over which specific row survives, unlike dropDuplicates()'s arbitrary choice.

questions.q: How does the row count of the result differ between groupBy().agg() and a window function with row_number()?
options: groupBy().agg() produces one row per group; a window function keeps every original row, just with an added ranking column
They always produce the exact same number of rows
A window function always produces fewer rows than the original DataFrame
groupBy().agg() always keeps every original row too
questions.explain: This is the core distinction the lesson draws between the two approaches.
